Linda Duncombe, a longtime banking executive and independent film producer, died on Sunday. She was 55.

The SAG-AFTRA Foundation, where Duncombe served on the board of directors, announced her death on Monday. She reportedly died of complications from a stroke shortly after being diagnosed with stage 2 lung cancer.

“We are devastated by the sudden loss of our dear friend and fellow Board member, Linda Duncombe,” Courtney B. Vance, president and chair of the SAG-AFTRA Foundation Board, wrote in a statement. “Linda was an extraordinary leader who brought a wealth of experience, influence and relationships to our Board, but what made her truly special was how generously she shared all of it.

“She believed wholeheartedly in the mission of this Foundation and in the importance of supporting the performers who bring stories to life,” Vance continued. “Linda had a remarkable ability to bring people together, open doors and turn her passion for this community into meaningful support for our work. She brought such warmth, wit and enthusiasm to everything she did. She will be deeply missed by our Board and staff, and by the many people whose lives she touched.”

Born on Feb. 10, 1971, in Australia, Duncombe later graduated from Western Sydney University and Harvard Business School. She then spent more than 35 years in banking, including at Citibank in Australia and later at the company’s subsidiary, Citi Fintech, in New York.

Duncombe moved to Los Angeles in 2019 to serve as the chief marketing, data and digital officer at City National Bank. There, she helped establish business, sponsorship and community relations with organizations such as SAG-AFTRA Foundation, the Recording Academy, the Motion Picture Television Fund and Tribeca Film Festival. She also led City National Bank’s efforts to deliver more than $1.8 billion in PPP loans to support the entertainment industry.

In 2022, she joined the SAG-AFTRA Foundation’s board of directors, where she “regularly attended Board meetings and educational programs, engaged with staff and fellow Board members, and drew upon her extensive relationships throughout the entertainment and business communities to raise awareness and critical support for the Foundation’s mission,” according to the organization.

Duncombe also joined the board of directors for EnCorps in 2025, a nonprofit organization founded by Sherry Lansing that focused on connecting STEM professionals with under-resourced public school students. She specifically worked on the EnCorps STEM Teachers Program.
As for her work as a producer, she worked on the films The Queen’s Jewels, Killing Time and Best Pancakes in the County.
Singer-songwriter EJAE was honored at Gyopo’s annual Chuseok Benefit.

The KPop Demon Hunters star is fresh off a whirlwind start to the year after the animated film dominated the awards circuit. EJAE earned herself Golden Globe, Grammy Award and an Oscar along the way. The singer was honored at Gyopo’s 8th annual Chuseok Benefit, which is sponsored by CJ ENM, late last month.

“I’m so honored to be recognized by GYOPO at this year’s Chuseok Benefit. It means so much to be surrounded by a community that celebrates the Korean diaspora and the many different ways we stay connected to our culture, because that connection is at the core of what I do,” she told The Hollywood Reporter.
“It’s been such a special afternoon,” she said. “I’m so proud to celebrate where we come from and what we’re creating together.”

The benefit, held Gyopo board member Ann Soh Woods’ private residence, brought together figures from art, design, entertainment and fashion, including Anicka Yi, Carol Lim,, Dumbfoundead, Jon Moon and fellow Demon Hunters stars Audrey Nuna and Kevin Woo. The event is held in early Autumn during the Korean harvest mon holiday Chuseok, which signifies a time to come together.

“We celebrate EJAE’s exhilarating artistic talent and its power to define an era of popular music and culture. EJAE’s journey to becoming a global music icon is one of perseverance and courage — complex, layered, and full of twists and turns,” Gyopo’s executive director Yoon Ju Ellie Lee said about the honoree.

She added, “Her story has resonated with millions across the globe, but it is the way she shares it, with clarity, honesty, humility and meaningfully contextualized within a diasporic Korean experience, that has touched the hearts of us at Gyopo. EJAE has used her platform to speak openly about her process, pressure, rejection and transformation. In times like these, we savor the opportunity to honor a kindred spirit such as EJAE.”

When he returned to host Saturday Night Live for a third time over the weekend, comedian Shane Gillis garnered a lot of attention for his monologue — and the response has been heated. One of the most vocal critics was Schitt’s Creek star Dan Levy, who posted an Instagram video on Sunday to explain why he took issue with the monologue, and to one part in particular.

The joke in question was when Gillis said, “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now? I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts?”
In his response video, captioned “Ffs,” Levy said in part, “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores; it makes the men calling them whores misogynists.”

His comments section was flooded with support, including from a handful of music stars. Jewel thanked Levy, while Wicked star Kristin Chenoweth posted a “100” emoji and Lisa Loeb commented alongside a fire emoji “Thank you.”

Maggie Baird, the activist mother of Billie Eilish and FINNEAS, shared Levy’s video to her Instagram Story with her own lengthy caption. “Thank you [Dan Levy]!” she started. “I literally gasped when [Shane Gillis] said this on [SNL]. I felt it physically (and was reminded of the horrible Bill Burr monologue),” she added, referencing Burr’s controversial 2020 appearance on the sketch comedy show, when he complained that white women had hijacked the “woke” movement and that Pride Month shouldn’t be so long. Baird continued: “I come from the sketch comedy world and am not squeamish around comedy, but how can men and comedy writers still think this is funny! It’s actually dangerous for women to promote this bullsh–.”
Flavor Flav also platformed Levy’s video, sharing an article about his response on X with the message: “Important allyship.”

Maren Morris added to the discourse in her own Instagram post as well, with the message “me being a wh0re at the gym” across a video of herself soundtracked by her song “be a bitch.” In the video, she throws up a middle finger to the camera and finished it off with the caption: “leave my gym short wedgie out of it.”

Gillis hosted Saturday’s show with Rosalía as the musical guest. In addition to it being his third time hosting, Gillis was also briefly a cast member of the show, but he was dismissed soon after the announcement of his casting when previous homophobic and racist jokes of his resurfaced.

Shakira wanted to end her European residency in Madrid on a high note, and for her 13th concert, she surrounded herself with great friends. Maluma, Laura Pausini, Beéle, Dani Martín and Bizarrap joined her for one last night, which also featured dancers from the Carnival of Barranquilla, a drone display and a visibly emotional Shakira bidding farewell.

“There has been a before and after for me. It’s all felt like a dream, and honestly, I don’t want to leave,” the Colombian superstar told the audience. “It’s going to be very, very hard to leave Spain again.”

Announced a week earlier as “The Last Dance,” Monday’s concert (Oct. 12) brought the residency to a total of 13 shows and concluded with four consecutive performances from Oct. 9-12. The finale also coincided with Spain’s National Day (Día de la Hispanidad), with Latin culture strongly present throughout the celebration.

“I’ve prepared so many, many surprises for you tonight,” Shakira teased shortly after starting the show. “Tonight, I’m not holding anything back. I’m going to give you everything, everything, everything I have, because there’s nothing like when a she-wolf meets her pack.”

The first surprise came with Maluma, who returned for the second night in a row to perform “Chantaje” and “Agua” alongside Shakira. “We’ve already done four songs together; we should form a group called Shaluma,” joked Shakira to her compatriot, who replied that he was ready to create many more songs with her.

Later, Shakira paused the show for several minutes to thank the audience and everyone who made possible what she described as one of “the most important” projects of her career. “This residency has been historic for me,” she said, adding that during these weeks, she had also gone through difficult moments, including her father’s health issues and other personal challenges. She said the audience gave her the strength to step on stage every night “with total joy and a full heart… You’ve made me feel like I’m just starting my career, and I will never forget that.”

The superstar then extended her gratitude to everyone who had been part of the show and Macondo Park, as well as Sony Music, Live Nation, her team, musicians and dancers. According to Shakira, more than 10,000 people worked on the production of the show and the themed city that was built around the stadium. She also gave a particularly heartfelt thank-you to her ex Antonio de la Rúa, a current collaborator, introducing him as “a great friend, a soul friend.” Shakira highlighted his support during the tour and his work behind the creation and details of the project.

Following her thank-yous, Laura Pausini took the stage as “the cherry on top,” as Shakira presented her. The Italian artist returned to the residency to perform a duet of “Antología,” as she had during one of the first nights of the residency. Before singing, she took a moment to offer some words, emphasizing what Shakira’s career represents for younger generations of artists. “You are a lesson for so many,” she said. “Just imagine our younger colleagues who see the immense example that you are of a long and very solid career.”

The next guest was Dani Martín, former lead singer of El Canto del Loco and one of the most recognized names in Spanish pop-rock, who joined her for “Te Dejo Madrid.” Shakira introduced him with a nod to the song’s lyrics: “Today, I’m going to sing this with a Madrileño who won’t break my heart.”

Beéle later joined her for a performance of “Algo Tú,” while several Carnival of Barranquilla dancers filled the stage, bringing a piece of her hometown’s celebration to a night that coincided with Spain’s National Day. For “Dai Dai,” the Ghetto Kids joined the celebration in a particularly colorful and vibrant evening.

The final performance also highlighted just how far the residency had come. “When they proposed doing eight concerts here in Madrid, I thought it would be impossible,” Shakira shared. “And look, today is our 13th show. Someone pinch me, please, so I know if this is real or not.” According to the artist, around 700,000 people attended the shows at the Shakira Stadium during the entire residency.

The energy remained high throughout the residency, both on stage and among the audience. Purple wigs and chain belts with coins became a recurring sight among attendees, who embraced some of the most iconic images from different stages of Shakira’s career. Near the end of the show, dozens of drones lit up the sky, first forming the shape of a she-wolf and then a giant “12+1,” the chosen way to mark the final night of the residency.

But one last surprise was still in store. Bizarrap took the stage for the grand finale, stepping behind the turntable to perform “Shakira: Bzrp Music Sessions, Vol. 53” with the singer, keeping the party alive until the final moments of “The Last Dance” and bringing nearly a month of Shakira in Madrid to a spectacular close.

William Shatner wasn’t sure if the audience would approve of his new documentary or not.

When the 95-year-old star took the stage at the Regal Times Square theater for the New York premiere of The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World he said “maybe you’ll like it, maybe you won’t.” But, the Captain Kirk actor declared, “you’re going to see a lovely film made by people who cared.”

Focusing on the original Star Trek series, which ran from 1966 to 1969, The Sixty-Year Mission is written and directed by Mark A. Altman, creator of the Inglorious Treksperts podcast. The documentary, which screened during New York Comic Con and hit select theaters this weekend, explores the show’s cultural impact and legacy, and also demonstrates how much it was a product of the political climate of the era in which it was made.

“I think audiences are pleasantly surprised that Sixty-Year Mission shows how the ‘60s shaped Star Trek,” Altman explains. For the film, Altman interviewed dozens of prominent fans and stars, from Shatner and Simon Pegg to Star Trek: The Next Generation stars Jonathan Frakes and Brent Spiner. The president’s niece—and Trek fan—Mary L. Trump praises the show’s pioneering representation, specifically Nichelle Nichols’ Lieutenant Uhura. George Takei, who played Sulu, gives a harrowing account of his time in an internment camp for Japanese Americans during World War II. Others discuss how characters like Spock became heroes for queer fans.

As has been well-documented, these considerations were important for Gene Roddenberry, the show’s creator, who died in 1991. He was a WWII veteran with a progressive bent despite years spent in traditionally conservative spaces like the US Army and the Los Angeles Police Department. Altman insists that “Captain Kirk was ‘JFK: Space Captain,’” and that President Kennedy’s idea of a New Frontier was the final frontier that Trek sought to explore.

Shatner, however, didn’t initially see the show that way at all. “I didn't think in those terms when they offered me the role,” says Shatner, who served as executive producer on Sixty-Year Mission. “I thought, ‘I got a regular paid job.’ Only later did the magic of Star Trek happen.”

Part of that magic, Shatner adds, is how “Star Trek had an effect on people’s lives.” Those people come from many backgrounds, and the show remained accessible because of the very special tension that existed within its politics, Altman explains. “Roddenberry was liberal on social issues but hard-nosed on defense, and that is absolutely what Star Trek is,” he says. “We need our phasers to defeat the Klingons, but we believe in a diverse crew.”

Karim Diané, who plays Jay-Den Kraag on Star Trek: Starfleet Academy, notes that as the person playing the first openly gay Klingon character in the franchise, he’s playing someone who means a lot to viewers. “I wish I could release the DMs because the love I've gotten is overwhelming,” Diané says.

Trek even had a point of view on AI that feels incredibly relevant in 2026 as Trump and Silicon Valley leaders talk about a new era of “superintelligence.” The franchise’s most recognizable AI—the android Data from Next Generation—was an ideal version of the technology. In that series Data consistently struggled to be understood, as both smarter than humans and incapable of emotional intelligence. One episode, “The Measure of a Man,” even addressed whether Data was his own being or merely property.

For Spiner, who played Data, AI’s modern incarnation is far from the thoughtful machine he portrayed. “If only AI could be what Data was: responsible, truly concerned about humanity, considering what serves humans best as opposed to what serves profit best,” he says.

Google’s screenless Fitbit Air made a splash, but it’s been three years since the company updated its display-equipped Charge 6. That older tracker is showing its age, lacking newer automatic workout detection, deeper health metrics, and an IP68 rating. That's where the new Fitbit Edge comes in.

Announced on Monday, it is the successor fitness tracker fans with a screen preference have been waiting for. It sits in a sweet spot at $180—not as costly as a Google Pixel Watch but offering a similar experience in a slimmer, pill-shaped design. And unlike the Pixel Watch, it's compatible with Android and iPhones via the Google Health app. Preorders are available now, and it goes on sale on October 27.

The Edge has a user-replaceable battery, a Fitbit first, aligning with Google’s efforts to make its Pixel Watch more repairable. (Likely also due to new battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union.) Repair options will vary by region and availability.

If you find the Pixel Watch’s round face too bulky, the Edge's capsule-shaped alternative might suit smaller wrists better. If the Charge 6’s 1.04-inch display was too small, the Edge upgrades it to a larger 1.34-inch screen. The difference is noticeable, and that extra real estate could make a real impact when glancing at your metrics mid-workout.

The Edge borrows a few more attributes from the Pixel Watch, including an altimeter that uses atmospheric pressure to measure elevation changes. That means it can record elevation gain and loss during outdoor activities, track floors climbed, and add more context to your outdoor stats. It also has a far-field skin temperature sensor, replacing the standard device temperature sensor found in other Fitbits. By bringing some of the Pixel Watch’s more advanced hardware to a fitness-first wearable, Google is giving the Edge a compelling middle-ground position in its lineup at a Fitbit-friendly price.

The Edge inherits the Fitbit Air’s improvements while restoring several Charge 6 features the screenless tracker lacks, including built-in GPS and electrical sensors that work with the electrocardiogram (ECG) app. You can also control music playback on a connected Bluetooth device, as you could with the Charge 6, and Google Maps turn-by-turn directions will arrive later this year.

Google also announced more advanced automatic activity tracking for the Edge, using Gemini Intelligence to identify up to 100 workout types. It can track more than 50 exercise modes, up from 40 on its predecessor. Google will also roll out these features to the Pixel Watch 5 and Air. If they work as promised, it means users won't have to log every activity manually.

With a Google Health Premium subscription, the Edge can track blood pressure trends without manual calibration and insulin resistance trends without requiring a blood draw. Google first announced these capabilities alongside the Pixel Watch 5's debut, but they only became available at the end of September. They’re also available on the Air, keeping Google’s screenless tracker up to date as its lineup expands.

The seven-day battery life remains unchanged, but it’s one of the Edge’s biggest advantages over the Pixel Watch. Like the Air, it takes about 90 minutes to fully charge, which is half an hour less than the Charge 6.

One odd omission is a near-field communication (NFC) sensor, which means the Edge doesn’t support contactless payments through Google Wallet. That’s a downgrade from the Charge 6 and a strange function to lose on a fitness tracker that Google is pitching as a step up from its basic Fitbits.

The Edge introduces new digital and analog clock faces, and the Canyon band color returns from the Pixel Watch 5, alongside five other band styles (Active Band, Active Sport Band, Performance Loop Band, Magnet Band, and Metal Links Band). The Stephen Curry collaboration ($220), which also appeared with the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5, is back in the same brown-orange color.

Alongside the Edge, Google is also giving the screenless Fitbit Air a visual upgrade with a new Metal Mesh band. It’s an even dressier strap than the polyurethane Elevated Modern Band. The Air may have initially been designed to disappear on your wrist, but the new band makes it a statement accessory.

If you’re all in on the screenless Fitbit Air, the Edge won’t change your mind. But if you’re not ready to give up a display, the Edge might be a compelling and affordable alternative for both iPhone and Android users. Stay tuned for our review.
Where it is from: Baffin Island, Nunavut, Canada

This wooden figurine was discovered in 1977 in an early house built by the ancestors of the Inuit on Baffin Island in northern Canada. The unique carving represents a person wearing European clothing and a cross on their chest. Dated to 1350, the figurine is the earliest Indigenous representation of a European anywhere in the Western Hemisphere and probably depicts a Norseman.

The tiny driftwood carving, which is currently on display at the Canadian Museum of History, measures just 2.1 inches (5.4 centimeters) tall. According to the museum, the featureless face and stumpy arms are common in 14th-century Inuit carvings, but the depiction of a non-Inuit is unique.

The mysterious figure wears a long robe or tunic with a cross on the front — a garment that is similar to those worn in the 11th to 13th centuries by Norse Christians from Greenland. The Norse sagas mention a place called "Helluland," which Leif Eriksson (also spelled Erikson) visited in the early 11th century and is most likely Baffin Island.

Around A.D. 1000, Norse explorers landed in what is now Newfoundland and set up camp at a site archaeologists call l'Anse aux Meadows. Wood buildings and remains from iron production are all that is left of the earliest European settlement in the Americas.

The Norse likely made multiple trips from Greenland to Canada over the centuries in order to trade metal and cloth with the Inuit's ancestors, known as the Thule, and procure walrus ivory in return, as European-origin artifacts have been found in early Inuit houses on Baffin Island. But the Norse eventually abandoned their westward trade routes, possibly due to the resistance of the Indigenous people and the long distance.

This wooden figurine may commemorate a meeting between the Inuit and the Norse and is especially important because it was crafted long before sustained contact in the late 15th century, according to the museum. It is also the earliest evidence of the Indigenous perspective of visitors from the east, revealing which characteristics of the Norse the artisan observed and felt were important to depict.
For more stunning archaeological discoveries, check out our Astonishing Artifacts archives.

After Guardian Australia put questions to the Daily Telegraph about Campion’s work with One Nation, the paper published an article about her new role in the party, which she told it was a “natural extension” of her career as a conservative commentator.
“Campion will continue to write her weekly column appearing every Saturday as a contributor,” the paper wrote.
After speaking to the Guardian, Campion subsequently posted to social media about her role, saying “the party is a phenomenon and unlike anything Australian politics has seen in a very long time”.

Campion worked as a media adviser to Joyce when he was deputy prime minister. The pair married in 2023. Joyce had announced in late 2017 that he and his first wife had separated and the Daily Telegraph subsequently published a photo of a pregnant Campion on its front page in February 2018.

In an appearance on the ABC’s Australian Story in August, Campion said she felt “suicidal” during a press conference called by the then prime minister, Malcolm Turnbull, after the story broke. The ABC issued an apology to Campion after the ABC News Instagram account published a clip from the episode with Campion discussing her experience of postpartum depression without disabling comments under the video.
Joyce, the federal MP for New England, defected from the Nationals to One Nation last December.

The revelation about Campion’s work for the party came after News24 reported that another high-profile former Coalition figure, the 2022 Liberal candidate for Warringah, Katherine Deves, would run as an upper house candidate in the NSW election. Deves had previously announced that she joined One Nation in September.

But after News24 reported that Deves – who said she had received death threats after comments she had made about transgender people surfaced during the 2022 campaign – would run as an upper house candidate, One Nation put out a statement saying it had only confirmed three candidates – Newman and the upper house candidates Stuart Bonds and Jeff Bacon, a firearms manufacturer based in Tamworth.

“We have received more than 800 [candidate] applications from community leaders, advocates and business people,” a spokesperson said. Campion told Guardian Australia she had no plans to run as a candidate for the party.
One Nation and the Saturday Telegraph were contacted for comment.
A bullet hole left in a bedroom door and DNA found in the barrel of the firearm have been scrutinised in court as Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial continues in Sydney.
Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

The prosecution argues the policeman disguised himself as an UberEats rider before entering Baird’s home, shooting him twice – in the base of the neck and the right temple – and then shooting Davies through the bedroom door.

But the defence alleges they were killed in two separate incidents when Lamarre-Condon was acting in “self-defence”. During the tussle with Baird, the firearm was flung across the room where it was picked up by Davies, who later shot himself in a struggle with the policeman, the defence argues.
Defence lawyer John Stratton SC cross-examined crime scene officer Greg Moon on Tuesday, questioning the prosecution’s version of events.

Stratton pointed to a swab taken from the barrel of the alleged murder weapon, which returned a DNA profile that partially matched Davies. He then noted the hole in the bedroom door, through which the prosecution alleges Davies was shot, tested negative for blood.

Stratton suggested: “The possibility or likelihood of biological material finding its way from a wound of the deceased through a hole in the door less than a centimetre in width and into the barrel of a gun … approaches zero.”
But Moon told the New South Wales supreme court he disagreed.
“I believe it can still happen,” he said.
The defence does not dispute the couple were shot.
A diagram from Dr Kendall Bailey, who conducted the postmortem examinations of both men, suggested a bullet entered Baird’s body at the base of his neck and exited just below his lip.
Asked by crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC about the effect of this wound, Bailey told the jury it did not pass through any major vessels of the neck or the vertebral column or windpipe.
But that did not mean it was insignificant, the court heard.
“It still would be a very nasty injury and that fracturing of the jaw is a very nasty injury,” she told the court.
While it is potentially survivable, those kinds of injuries can be painful and cause some to pass out, though others may not lose consciousness, Bailey explained.
Hatfield then asked if person with those injuries could speak.
The bullet went through the jaw and the base of the tongue, Bailey said, adding: “I don’t think anyone with that injury would be making any meaningful vocalisations.
“They could make a noise but that would be nothing that would be coherent,” she said.
Bailey then explained the shot that entered the temple would go through the brain, where it would incapacitate a person.

Asked if that person would then be able to fling a gun to the other side of the room, she said the body could make some involuntary movements but “I don’t think that person is making any conscious movements”.
CT scans of Baird and Davies’ skulls showing the damage caused by the bullets were presented to the jury on Thursday.

Forensic radiologist Dr James Raleigh explained to the court there was a hole in the right side of Baird’s head at the temple region and multiple small bone fragments “presumably from that damage were run in a line across the inside of the skull”.
Davies’ wound was located in his face just above the left eyebrow, which Raleigh agreed was consistent with a bullet hole.
Two wounds on Davies’ thigh were consistent with a “single-bladed weapon”, Bailey said.
But she agreed those injuries likely took place after or at the time of death.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

The Tampa Bay bullpen ran out of gas late Monday night. After seven innings of grind-it-out baseball in St. Petersburg, the Cleveland Guardians broke loose with five runs over the final two frames to take Game 1 of the ALCS, 7-3.

With two outs in the opening frame, Junior Caminero and Jonny DeLuca ripped consecutive RBI knocks to put Tampa Bay up 2-0. Rays starter Drew Rasmussen kept that lead strong through five innings, punching out seven.
Cleveland finally cracked Rasmussen in the sixth when Chase DeLauter jumped on a heater and launched an opposite-field solo shot over the right-center wall.
Patrick Bailey pulled Cleveland even leading off the seventh, hooking a solo blast down the right-field line to end Rasmussen's night at 2-2.

The Guardians kept the heat on in the eighth against Tyler Wells and Ian Seymour. Ramirez started the fire with a hustle infield single, DeLauter ripped a double down the line, and Nathaniel Lowe laced a go-ahead, two-run single to make it 4-2.
Tampa Bay answered in the bottom of the eighth when pinch-hitter Cedric Mullins ambushed Erik Sabrowski with a solo shot to right, trimming the deficit to 4-3.
Then Jose Ramirez delivered the knockout blow.

Capping a 3-for-5 night with two runs scored, Cleveland's veteran third baseman stepped in with two outs in the ninth and lined an RBI single into right off Cole Sulser to make it 5-3. After Sulser walked DeLauter, Kevin Kelly entered to face Jo Adell. The mid-season acquisition stepped up to the big moment, ripping a two-run double down the third-base line to put the contest on ice at 7-3.
Cleveland pounded out 14 hits against six Tampa Bay arms, with Ramirez and DeLauter combining for six knocks before Cade Smith slammed the door on six pitches.
The Rays entered Monday riding high after sweeping the Yankees, but they left the yard with all the pressure.
Game 2 is Tuesday night at Tropicana Field.

The Philadelphia Eagles flew all the way across the Atlantic Ocean just to hand a victory to the Jacksonville Jaguars. Unsurprisingly, former All-Pro cornerback Asante Samuel has seen enough.
Eight seconds left, a one-point lead, and a squib kick sealed it. Instead, Nick Sirianni gifted Jacksonville a live return, setting up an improbable walk-off win.
Speaking on the "Say What Needs To Be Said" show, Samuel put Sunday's 19-17 collapse squarely on Philadelphia's head coach.

"You lost the game for your team," Samuel said. "Of course, the team was going to have his back and say, 'No, coach, it's not on you. It's on us.' But all the coach had to do was call a squib kick. A squib kick at the end of the game is normal and done all the freaking time."
Samuel torched Sirianni for his lack of awareness in crunch time.

"Nick Sirianni must have had a lapse in his brain or something and wasn't paying attention for him to miss out on that situation," Samuel said. "There's no way your team fights that hard for that long, and you let your team down by not making sure the right call is being made."

The blunder erased what should have been a gritty road win. Down Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith to hamstring injuries, Philadelphia took a 17-16 lead with eight seconds left on Jake Elliott's 48-yard field goal.
Jacksonville's Ameer Abdullah responded by fielding a clean kickoff, ripping off a 53-yard return, and setting up Cam Little's walk-off 57-yarder as time expired.
The loss dropped Philadelphia to 2-3 while pushing the Jags to their third-straight victory.
Sirianni fell on his sword Sunday right after the final whistle.

"I didn't make the right decision and I lost us that game," Sirianni told reporters. "And that's what I said to our guys. What hurts there is that the guys fought so hard, and then I don't make the decision that I should make at the end of the game and I cost us that game and I put that fully on me."
When asked why Philadelphia left eight seconds on the board before Elliott's kick, Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts made it clear game management was outside his control.

"It’s not my place, and we’re prepared, I’m prepared as a quarterback to not worry about those things," Hurts told reporters Monday. "So I’m honoring a play call, honoring the things that are coming in the game. When I’m up at night, yeah, I think about, 'Man, should I have said something, or should I have took a step back and said, "Wait"?' But ultimately, there’s a commitment to that and going out there and executing. And so this was one where it did not work in our favor."
Sirianni doubled down Monday, shutting down any idea that Hurts should have overruled the sideline.

"Jalen’s playing," Sirianni told reporters. "We’re coaching and calling the plays, and Jalen’s got to go execute what we call in that moment, 100 percent. We’re not asking him to make play calls in that scenario. He’s already got enough to worry about to go out and execute. That’s where we were there in that situation."
Sirianni can preach staying in your lane all day, but Hurts is losing sleep over brain-dead strategy, and Samuel wants the head coach held to the fire.

A New York man pleaded guilty to murdering and dismembering his ex-girlfriend and putting her severed head in a suitcase with a flower after she ended their relationship, later telling investigators she had "played me like a sucker," according to authorities.
Damon Foy, 50, of Kerhonkson, pleaded guilty last week to second-degree murder in the 2024 death of Alberta Dale, 44, of Pennsylvania, according to the Ulster County District Attorney's Office.
Between March 31 and April 1, 2024, Foy killed and dismembered Dale and was in the process of disposing of her body when law enforcement intervened, according to the district attorney's office.

The Ulster County Sheriff's Office began investigating on April 1, 2024, after Dale's family members in Pennsylvania contacted law enforcement because they were concerned about her well-being, the district attorney's office said. Deputies first conducted a welfare check before launching a missing person investigation.

Deputies first went to Foy’s apartment on April 1, 2024, and found Dale’s car, according to the New York Post. The next day, deputies returned to question Foy after a member of the public found Dale’s phone on the side of the road and turned it in to authorities, leading investigators to suspect potential foul play.

"She’s in there," Foy whispered to investigators, when they arrived at his home during the missing person investigation. "I killed her," he added, according to court documents cited by the New York Post.
Investigators obtained a search warrant for Foy's home and found a suitcase in a closet that contained the victim's remains. Foy was then arrested and charged in connection with Dale's death.
After shining a flashlight on the suitcase, investigators "immediately noticed what appeared to be dried blood," according to the documents.
"Officers opened the defendant’s suitcase and found Alberta Dale’s partial dismembered remains, including her severed head," the court documents read, according to the New York Post.
"The remaining portions of her dismembered body were not located during the execution of the search warrant," the documents add.
When he was later interviewed, Foy told investigators he "loved her," according to the documents.

"The only thing she kept doing after the time throughout the whole relationship was just play me, play me like a fool, play me like a sucker, and just took advantage of the whole f–king system," he said.

"That’s it. I was told to leave my own home. I was told to leave my own f–king home, not a bill in her name, and I was told to leave my own f–king home. Get out. Then it all started coming clearer to me," he added.
When asked about the flower in the suitcase, Foy only said he was thinking about "what still happened last night to take s— over the top."
Foy had a history of domestic violence against Dale, according to court documents cited by the New York Post.
A previous domestic incident involved a gun, and investigators had also observed an axe at Foy’s property when they were searching for Dale.
Dale had previously warned authorities that "if she went missing it was because [Foy] killed her," according to the court documents.
Under a plea agreement, Foy is expected to receive 23 years to life behind bars, with a minimum term two years shorter than the maximum of 25 years to life, according to the Daily Freeman.
Chief Assistant District Attorney Liz Culmone-Mills told the outlet that the agreement was backed by Dale’s family.
"The District Attorney’s Office would not be making this recommendation were it not for Alberta Dale’s family," Culmone-Mills told the outlet.
Foy is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. 16.

"The total selfish disregard for the life and dignity of another person is at the heart of domestic violence; Damon Foy has shown that to us," District Attorney Emmanuel C. Nneji said in a statement. "We must recognize in our laws the rights of victims of domestic violence to be physically, psychologically, and emotionally safe from their tormentors and the dangers specifically targeted for them, and demand procedures that actually protect victims for real, not just on paper."
United States President Donald Trump has insisted that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, as he called on both sides to end the “ridiculous” war.

Trump’s comments on Monday came even as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces had struck at least six Ukrainian energy facilities since the US president declared the truce on Sunday.
“Well, they agreed,” Trump told reporters, referring to Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin. “Because I said, ‘You agree’. That’s why they agreed, because I said they agree.”
When pressed about the Russian strikes, Trump said, “Well, I’d have to look at it and see, because there’s been violations on both sides.”

The US president called the war, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a “disaster” and claimed, without offering evidence, that at least 32,000 people had been killed this month alone.
“All I know is that Zelenskyy and Putin have to get together and end that ridiculous war,” he said.

Trump had blindsided Kyiv and its European allies when he announced the purported energy ceasefire on Sunday. The announcement came two days after he temporarily eased US sanctions on Russian diesel, a move that drew outrage in Europe and Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said it reversed years of Western efforts to isolate Russia’s economy and would only embolden Putin.

Lawmakers from both major parties in the United States have also said the diesel decision appears to violate US law. Several Republicans have objected that it undercuts a law Trump himself signed to tighten restrictions on Moscow.

Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire and had carried out no attacks on Russian refineries overnight. He said Kyiv was prepared to sign “guarantees to make sure they can be trusted”.
But he said it was “increasingly evident” that Moscow would not comply.

“Today alone, the Russians have attacked 6 energy facilities in Ukraine. 33 people were wounded across the country,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. “This is what happens when Russia sees the prospect of higher revenues for its war machine.”
Russia, however, has rejected any pause in fighting, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov promising to press ahead with the military campaign.

“I do not think he deserves a respite,” he said of Zelenskyy. “I don’t think we’ll be buying into assurances and promises again.” Russia, he added, would continue to pursue the goals of what it calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.

Trump, meanwhile, has portrayed Ukraine, rather than Russia, as the main obstacle to peace. He has said that Putin is more eager on a deal than Zelenskyy, and has called on Ukrainians to vote their president out of office – an unusually harsh turn in a relationship that has been strained since Trump returned to the White House in 2025.
Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher, reporting from Washington, DC, said Trump has previously announced agreements between Russia and Ukraine that never materialised.

“He says he wants to protect industries in the US like farmers and ranchers, and to do that he needs the price to go down. But it seems that he thinks there’s a deal, but no one else is sure that there actually is one,” Fisher said.
The latest announcement, according to our correspondent, appeared to be driven by Trump’s desire to bring down diesel prices before the US midterm elections on November 3.
Most polls predict that Republicans will lose control of Congress as voters grow frustrated with rising prices, particularly for petrol.

An opinion survey published on October 1 by the Associated Press news agency and the University of Chicago suggested that 65 percent of US adults blame the White House for the high cost of living, especially Trump’s tariff policies and his new war against Iran.
Ukraine’s European allies, meanwhile, voiced scepticism about the energy ceasefire and approved the largest set of European Union sanctions since Russia’s 2022 invasion.
The bloc’s foreign ministers added some 1,569 people and businesses to the bloc’s sanctions list to maintain the pressure on Moscow.
“Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, which is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in Berlin.

A cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets in France has raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F), spoiling food and causing fires at several stores.
Top retailers Intermarche, Cooperative U, E Leclerc and others confirmed the “unprecedented” cyberattack on Monday.
At least 300 shops of Intermarche or its Netto brand were targeted, along with more than 100 Cooperative U outlets, the retailers told the AFP news agency.
Carrefour said 80 supermarkets were affected, while Monoprix said about 5 percent of its roughly 490 stores were hit. E Leclerc said several of its stores were targeted.
The Paris prosecutor’s office said the “large-scale” attack had affected “connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France”. It led to food losses and fires, the office said.
The attack prompted Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to order France’s National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate, a person in his office told the Reuters news agency.
The source said France was coordinating with European counterparts because other countries could also be affected, adding that authorities were assessing whether other French companies were at risk.

There was no immediate estimate of industry-wide losses, but Intermarche CEO Thierry Cotillard told BFM TV the “unprecedented” attack would represent losses amounting to “tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day”.

According to BFM TV, the hackers had “managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores”. The action resulted in the “destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products”, it said.
Intermarche told AFP that affected stores would have to “throw away all of the products” that were fresh or frozen.
Dominique Schelcher, chief executive of Cooperative U, said the attack had disrupted refrigeration systems since Sunday night.
“Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is extremely serious and is unprecedented. It is unacceptable,” he wrote on X.
He said the company’s teams were working to restore normal operations as quickly as possible, and that an investigation would be needed to “shed full light on this attack”.

Supermarket cold aisles are typically run by control panels that manage an entire store’s fridges and freezers and can be accessed over the internet, which lets maintenance companies adjust them from anywhere.
The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss.
Danfoss said it was “aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems”.
The affected units “were running outdated firmware”, the company said, adding that it had “long advised customers” to keep their systems updated and replace older equipment.
The attack came after cybersecurity firm Claroty published research on August 9 describing vulnerabilities in Danfoss systems that could allow attackers to bypass authentication.
France’s retail federation, known as the FCD, called on Danfoss to provide “full transparency”.
It said some affected stores were already operating again.
Felix Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research, told Reuters that Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium had also been affected.
The attack resembles disruptions in late August at about a dozen US military commissaries, where problems with refrigeration systems led to food losses.

United States Archbishop Timothy Broglio has urged Catholics who are members of the country’s armed forces not to take part in a planned public execution by firing squad, saying that it violates the teachings of the church.

Broglio released a strongly worded statement on Monday raising a series of concerns about the US military’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army major who killed 13 people during a shooting attack at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.
“I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” Broglio said.
He also asked whether the US wants to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries”.
The plan to livestream the execution on December 3 was announced last week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who characterised the spectacle as deterrence.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told the right-wing media outlet Real America’s Voice.
But the proposal has sparked backlash from lawmakers, rights groups and critics who warn that a publicly broadcast killing is not only unethical but could also be used as anti-US propaganda.

Hasan, now aged 56, was shot by the police during the 2009 Fort Hood attack and is now wheelchair-bound. Critics fear livestreaming Hasan’s death could turn him into a symbol for armed groups that may be hostile to the US.
Cardinal Blase J Cupich, the archbishop of Chicago, also condemned the plan to livestream the execution in a social media post on Monday, questioning the example it could set for children.

“Capital punishment is unacceptable in any case,” he said. “The planned broadcast of the taking of a life by firing squad is nothing short of performative barbarism. Do we really want our children, who will inevitably view it, exposed to the pornography of a state-sponsored slaying?”
Hegseth has said he wants the execution to take place at the same time and location as the 2009 shooting spree, and described using military members to carry out the death penalty.
“It hadn’t been since World War II since we’ve done that,” Hegseth said of the firing squad. “Well, I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win.”
The last US military execution by firing squad was of Eddie Slovik, who was accused of desertion in 1945. He was the only US soldier to have such a sentence carried out for abandoning his post.
In Monday’s statement, Broglio also questioned the reasoning behind putting service members on camera to carry out Hasan’s death. He hinted that it could harm the US military’s image abroad.

“The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio wrote. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheel chair to the whole world?”
Without mentioning Hasan’s case specifically, Pope Leo also released a statement on Saturday condemning the death penalty.
“The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” he said in a social media post.

“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.”
President Donald Trump, who oversaw an unprecedented spike in federal executions during his first term in office, has approved Hasan’s execution.
Still, on Saturday, he indicated that he has not decided whether to proceed with a livestream.
“There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters. “I’ll make a decision.”

Since the start of his second term as president, Trump has pushed for the increased use of the federal death penalty. In April, he also approved additional methods to carry out the death penalty, including the firing squad.
In the past, Trump has also floated the death penalty as a punishment for crimes ranging from drug dealing to sedition, a term he has invoked against political rivals.
Hurricane Simon lashed vulnerable resorts and towns along Mexico's Pacific Coast on Sunday as it moved parallel to the shoreline, despite weakening to a category 3 storm.
"Additional weakening is forecast but Simon is still expected to be a strong hurricane as it passes near the coast of west-central Mexico tonight," the US National Hurricane Center's advisory said.
Simon is expected to move farther offshore on Monday before turning back towards Mexico's coast on Wednesday, it said.

Mexican authorities have placed 28 municipalities across the states of Jalisco and Colima under the highest cyclone alert level. Another 93 municipalities were under high alert, according to civil protection bulletins.

The hurricane's center closed in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rains were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Puerto Vallarta is a popular tourist destination in Jalisco. Apart from the resorts, several Mexicans live in communities inland and uphill, in houses that may not be able to weather the storm.
Experts believe the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.

"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin said.

"They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."
In Manzanillo, residents waded through flooded streets on Sunday morning as soldiers helped rescue locals from the overnight rainfall.
"The beds, the refrigerators, the stoves, all the furniture got wet. The whole house flooded," Cecilia Palomar told Reuters outside her home.
"My mother doesn't want to leave. We took her to my brother's, to higher ground. She's an elderly woman, but she doesn't want to leave. She doesn't want to be away from her home."
Airport closed, authorities urge caution
Puerto Vallarta International Airport was closed temporarily while authorities suspended non-essential activities.
They also established emergency shelters in threatened coastal communities.
Earlier on Sunday, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum had urged residents of coastal communities in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to remain indoors ahead of the storm.
Hurricane Simon has come days after Hurricane Polo struck Mexico's Baja California Peninsula as a Category 2 storm, knocking down power lines and flooding the streets.

Omid, whose real name cannot be used, signed up to join Iran's security forces when he was 18 years old and harbored "a deep commitment to my country." At the academy, Omid told DW, cadets were under the regime's control "day and night," from their military training through the daily prayers and speeches.
"They mold the minds of the young cadets," Omid said.

Some of these recruits, Omid said, eventually rise through the ranks of Iran's security apparatus to join an elite cadre of officers who plot missions, abductions and assassinations inside and outside of Iran — and have access to unlimited resources and personnel. And, he said, he attended their meetings.

When Omid, a burly man who carries scars accumulated during his decades-long service as a commander with Iran's elite special forces, reached out in early 2026, deliberations ensued: Could he have been sent to feed DW misinformation and lies to discredit the broadcaster, whose Farsi service is officially sanctioned in Iran? Could he be trying to harm DW or its Iranian employees?

Over the course of months, journalists from DW's investigative unit and Persian department corresponded with him. Omid shared records and photos of his training, which ranged from sniper practice and surveillance to street fighting, riot control and parachuting courses. He also provided photos and videos, documents and locations of a secret monitoring center and housing compounds reserved for high-ranking members of the Iranian security forces.
United in their absolute loyalty to Iran's supreme leader, he said, a clandestine circle of high-ranking officers plot and execute the murder and abductions of the regime's opponents.

Omid's testimony offered a rare insight into Iran's powerful and opaque security apparatus — and into the lives of the men at the core of the Islamic Republic — allowing DW to piece together a picture of how the regime has maintained deeply loyal forces despite widespread protest movements, international sanctions, rising inflation and recent attacks by its two main enemies, Israel and the United States, that eliminated much of its top military and political leadership.

DW corroborated substantial parts of Omid's account with documents, photos, videos and interviews with experts. An intermediary connected the investigative team with a second high-ranking defector, whose account corroborated key details provided by Omid. Though DW confirmed both men's identities, we are withholding certain details to protect them and their families.
In the past, Iran has gone after dissidents and opposition activists abroad, including journalists.
We asked the Embassy of Iran in Berlin and the Supreme Leader’s Office to respond to our findings. The Supreme Leader's Office did not reply.
The embassy in Berlin declined to address the individual allegations, stating that "the Islamic Republic of Iran firmly rejects these allegations and the conclusions drawn from them."

As a high-ranking member of the special forces, Omid had access to the privileges the regime often bestows upon its own: From financial incentives and lucrative economic contracts for their own enterprises to special housing compounds, with their own mosques, schools and hospitals, where personal satellite dishes are banned and religious observance is enforced.

These privileges have their price, Omid said: "control, nothing but control." Officers are tightly monitored. "You're not allowed to just attend a wedding or travel," he said. "They confiscate your passport; they even decide which schools your children are allowed to attend."

The control extends to soldiers' prospective partners, who are first vetted by the regime. Even then, Omid said, he was not allowed to share the true nature of his work with his wife. That, he said, "really eats away at you."

By separating such agents from regular Iranians, the regime can keep a closer eye on its forces, said Saeid Golkar, political scientist at the University of Tennessee, who has extensively researched the command structure of the Islamic Republic's security apparatus. "They can create peer pressure and indoctrinate much more effectively," Golkar told DW.
And, Golkar said, security forces who are largely segregated from regular Iranians are less likely to balk at using force against their civilian compatriots.
A defector from Iran's intelligence agency

A month into DW's interactions with Omid, an intermediary connected us with another high-ranking defector. The man, whom we're calling Reza, worked with the Information Ministry, Iran's intelligence agency.

Like many who are recruited into the security apparatus, Reza hails from a religious family: He grinned as he showed DW a picture on his phone of himself as a young man, sporting the long beard and turban favored by the devout in Iran.
Many of his relatives, he said, still occupy prominent positions in the Iranian regime.

In the early days, he was an ardent supporter of the regime and would sometimes cry during prayers, he said, knowing that he was serving his people and the Islamic Republic and "might even die as a martyr for Islam."

Reza said he slowly turned against the regime as he witnessed the clampdown on protesters. Over the years, officers have shot, arrested and beaten Iranians protesting the country's deteriorating living conditions and strict "morality" laws.

On the evening of January 8, amid an almost total internet shutdown, security forces opened fire on Iranians protesting widespread shortages and spiking inflation. The extent of the massacre slowly came to light as images trickled out of the country documenting the regime's atrocities.

Thousands of protesters were killed across Iran. Both Omid and Reza said the mass killings which, human rights organizations report, included the shooting of unarmed protesters in hospital beds — had horrified them.
Indeed, this ongoing brutality ultimately led them to speak with DW.
Omid was adamant that he had never shot at protesters nor ordered his subordinates to do so, although DW is unable to corroborate this.
When pressed, he conceded that he had witnessed the killing of demonstrators.

Reza said the guilt he carried after having "wasted 10, 11 years serving a cruel system" compelled him to speak out despite the risk to him and his family. "The truth is: When your opponent is a regime that doesn't adhere to any moral values, you need to be prepared for anything," he said.

Omid and Reza discussed secret command centers that are central to clamping down on protests. High-ranking members of all units and agencies gather in a monitoring room where, Omid and Reza say, huge monitors on the walls display real-time feeds from countless CCTV cameras around the capital, Tehran. They say there are other such rooms around the country.

Protest marches are also monitored from above by drones. And, Reza said, "information from forces on the ground and from Twitter, Telegram and other social networks, as well as information obtained through surveillance and interception devices — all this information is collected there."
Plainclothes agents often infiltrate protest groups. Omid said such agents were sometimes used to redirect protest marches to places where security forces lie in wait.
A representative of Iran's supreme leader "had a free hand" in ordering operations from within the command center, Omid said, as well as deciding "how harshly the protesters should be dealt with."

When regular police can no longer quell demonstrations, Omid and Reza said, elite units from the Revolutionary Guard and police, often clad entirely in black, their faces hidden behind balaclavas, are sent in to finish the job.
Human rights organizations have documented the use of automatic and semiautomatic machine guns and even heavy machine guns mounted on top of pickup trucks to clamp down on protests.

"The fact that the security forces are equipped with military-grade firearms that were designed for combat situations, for responding to protests, shows that the killings of protesters in the country are intended," finds Amnesty International Iran researcher Raha Bahreini, the author of a recent report analyzing the regime's chain of command during the 2022 protests following the death of Jina Mahsa Amini in custody.

After months of correspondence, Omid pointed DW to an outwardly unremarkable location in Shahr-e Rey, on the outskirts of Tehran: A prayer hall sandwiched between an occupational therapy practice and a pharmacy. Though the prayer hall is named Beit al Shohada, or the house of martyrs, Omid said many officers call the place Dakhme, meaning crypt or tomb.

Omid described how high-ranking officers met under Dakhme's corrugated iron roof to plot off-the-books operations that bypass government structures. He said he had attended several meetings at Dakhme "where decisions about murder are made: It's a killing machine."

Though Omid insisted repeatedly that he had only attended the meetings because he had been ordered to by his higher-ups and he had never taken part in any of the operations plotted at Dakhme, he listed murders and abductions within and outside of Iran that he said were planned there. DW could not verify these cases but found that some of the people named had indeed died under unresolved circumstances.

Several experts DW contacted knew of Dakhme in connection with a murder attempt on an adviser to a reformist president over two decades ago. Others had never heard of Dakhme. No one DW spoke with could confirm its continued operation.

Experts agree that a facility such as Dakhme is plausible. "The Islamic Republic probably feels more of a need now to have these types of groups," Miad Maleki, a former US Treasury official who until recently designed US sanctions programs targeting Iran, told DW.
Indeed, Maleki said, military operations planned covertly at Dakhme would likely give the regime plausible deniability in cases of killings.

Because of the secrecy surrounding Dakhme, much of the following is based only on Omid's accounts and the rare images DW obtained of religious ceremonies inside the hall. The secret meetings usually kick off under the guise of religious ceremonies and rituals, he said, in a large hall often adorned with green drapes and religious banners. After a communal dinner, only those in the inner circle stay.

Those who remain hand over their mobile phones, which are locked away. Then, Omid said, "seasoned specialists from Iran's special forces and intelligence operation " discuss murder and abductions late into the night.

"For these people, a person's position isn't that important," Omid said. "If they consider someone a threat to the supreme leader of the Islamic Republic, they take it extremely seriously and take action."
After each operation, Omid said, the men return to their respective roles within Iran's security apparatus, until they gather again to defend the Islamic Republic at any cost.

Around 51% of the population of the United States is female, but that is not reflected in the makeup of the US Congress, where only 28.4% of the members are women. Nevertheless, with 152 women in total sitting in the House of Representatives and Senate, the number is higher than it has ever been in the history of the United States. The number of female governors of the 50 US states is also currently higher than ever before: Some 14 of them — 28% — are women.

There are a number of reasons why there are still comparatively few female representatives in the US Congress. "Some of them are structural: There are rules and processes in place in our political system that make it harder for any newcomers to break in," said Kelly Dittmar, director of research at the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. "Historically, women were newcomers."

Seats in the Senate only come up for election every six years. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms, but there is no limit to the number of times they can stand for reelection, so in theory they can stay in office for decades.

Also, as Dittmar pointed out, election campaigns in the US are very expensive. Women have historically been less able to access networks of rich donors — who, like many party leaders, are still most likely to be men. Leading male politicians are also more likely to recruit men to stand as new candidates. Finally, cultural biases also play a role — the "stereotypes and expectations about what women can and should do."

The elections on November 3 will decide whether more or fewer women will sit in the US Congress over the next two years. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election in the midterms. And in 36 states, the citizens will also decide who will move into the governor's mansion.
House of Representatives: Female Democrats outnumber female Republicans three to one

In the House, 125 of the 435 representatives are women. As in the Senate, and also with the gubernatorial posts, they are not evenly distributed between the two parties: There are more women among the Democrats than among the Republicans. At present, there are 95 women sitting as representatives for the Democrats, and 30 for the Republicans.

"There is a far less robust support infrastructure for women within the Republican Party," said Dittmar. She said that organizations that specifically recruit, train and fund women candidates are almost all either on the Democrat side, or nonpartisan.

"A lot of the [Republican] party leaders don't see an electoral incentive or pressure" to recruit more women, she added. Diversity is more important to Democrat voters, who place greater value on seeing women among their elected representatives.

The Republicans currently have a majority in the House of Representatives, which means that they also get to appoint the speaker, or majority leader. At the moment, the position is held by Mike Johnson. Only one woman has held this powerful post to date: Nancy Pelosi, who was the Democrats' speaker from 2007 to 2011, and again from 2019 to 2023.

Women currently constitute 27% of the US Senate — 16 Democrats and 11 Republicans. Each of the 50 states is represented by two senators. The term of office is longer in this chamber of the US Congress, and the majority of the officials here represent many more voters than the representatives in the lower house.

According to Dittmar, it's even harder for women to win a seat in the Senate. "With the Senate, it's an opportunity and timing issue," she said. Each seat comes up for election every six years. There are 100 in total, and every two years only a third of them are available. Little opportunity, then, for women who have not previously sat in the Senate to advance.

A state-wide senatorial election campaign is also more expensive than the equivalent campaign for a seat in the House of Representatives — and studies indicate that female candidates are generally less wealthy than their male counterparts.

For one senatorial candidate, the November midterms could prove historic. If the Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins in Minnesota, she will be the first Native American woman to sit in the US Senate. Flanagan is Ojibwe, otherwise known as Chippewa, an Indigenous people from the Great Lakes region spanning the US and Canada.

Flanagan currently holds the post of lieutenant governor of Minnesota. Polls suggest that her chances are good. She has a slight lead over her rival, the Republican Michele Tafoya, previously a sports reporter and adviser to conservative politicians.

Ten of the current 14 female governors are Democrats, while four are Republicans. Six of the 14 are standing again, including Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the governor of Arkansas, who was President Donald Trump's press secretary during his first term in office.

For the first time in US history, a Black woman may be elected state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Tim Walz — Kamala Harris' vice-presidential candidate in the 2024 election — is not standing for reelection. The main rivals for his seat are the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the (Black) Republican Lisa DeMuth. Meanwhile, the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is running for governor of the state of Georgia.

Dittmar doesn't think DeMuth will win in Minnesota — the state is regarded as solidly Democrat. And Klobuchar is well known among the people there; she has represented Minnesota in the US Senate since 2007.

But in Georgia, according to Dittmar, it's a different story: "That race is considered a toss-up, 50-50." Dittmar believes that Bottoms "absolutely has a chance to be the first Black woman governor." Former President Barack Obama is her most prominent supporter, while President Trump has declared his support for the Republican candidate, Rick Jackson.
