For independent parts store owners, a national strategy earns its value at the local counter – when inventory meets demand, deliveries keep repair bays moving and employees turn customer relationships into repeat business. Connecting NAPA’s investments to those everyday results was the central message of the 2026 NAPA Store Owner and Field Sales Meeting, held Sept. 21-24 in Atlanta.

Bringing together owners from across the country, the meeting offered direct access to NAPA leadership, business insights and initiatives addressing network optimization, sales enablement and operational excellence. Throughout the opening session, speakers emphasized that progress depends on corporate support and owners’ local knowledge working together.

During the event’s opening session, Tom Skov, executive VP Sales, established that tone by encouraging attendees to “assume positive intention” while speaking candidly about challenges. He acknowledged that NAPA needs owner feedback to improve and urged participants to turn conference discussions into practical solutions.
“Identifying problems and identifying solutions to those problems is exactly what we need from this group over the next couple of days,” Skov said.

Court Carruthers, introduced as CEO-elect General Parts Company, reinforced that invitation. His approach centers on listening, learning from the field and ensuring company priorities help owners compete. He reaffirmed the independent owner model, pointing to community relationships and entrepreneurial investment that a corporation cannot replicate.

Carruthers said the planned separation of Motion would sharpen GPC’s automotive focus, concentrating attention and investment on the aftermarket. Supply chain improvements, digital tools, catalog capabilities and simpler execution would support that direction.

Alain Masse, president of North American Automotive, called for faster progress while acknowledging inconsistent support and past underinvestment. He outlined priorities including supply chain modernization, better technology and customer experience, dedicated owner support and clearer expansion opportunities.
“NAPA Drive 2030 only works with you in it, inside it and not beside it,” Masse said.

David Pley, who leads NAPA’s transformation effort, explained how owner input is shaping execution. Using a NASCAR analogy, he described owners as drivers supported by category, pricing, catalog and transformation teams: “One car, one team, one goal.”

Working with an advisory council of 22 owners, NAPA identified immediate priorities around go-to-market improvements, catalog capabilities and fill rates. Additional work addresses technology, payments, financing, underperforming stores and distribution network optimization.

Pley reported progress across nine priorities and emphasized a “say-do relationship”—connecting commitments to visible action. He highlighted Boost’s coordinated inventory and financing support, along with investment in ISO Excellence and a digital platform intended to consolidate information and assistance.

Chris Kinghorn, senior vice president, sales enablement & strategy, shifted the discussion to measuring local opportunity. Sales and profit matter, he said, but market share helps owners understand how much business remains available nearby.
“Sales tell you how you did. Share tells you how you played,” Kinghorn said.

NAPA is developing market-share reporting tools, with reports piloted through advisory council members. Meanwhile, Kinghorn encouraged owners to define realistic service areas and focus resources on customers with strong growth potential. Dependable parts supply establishes credibility; training, business tools and support help deepen the relationship.
“When we help them build their business, we’re building ours,” he said.
Developing the People Behind Performance

NAPA Academy supplied a practical example of that investment in capability. Cassie Bell, senior vice president of HR, introduced training developed for company-owned stores and now being extended to independent owners.

The initial offering focuses on store managers, combining 10- to 20-minute online courses with a downloadable reference guide. Financial results, team development, operational excellence and customer service form the curriculum’s foundation.

Jesse Parrish, director of learning and development, explained that resources reflect practices observed in high-performing stores. Relevant lessons also benefit counter employees. Participation is voluntary, with courses accessible through NAPA Connect.

Closing the session, Skov returned to the purpose behind the initiatives: helping owners build profitable businesses that strengthen their communities. He urged attendees to carry constructive feedback into the breakout sessions.
“We want to build these businesses,” Skov said, emphasizing NAPA’s commitment to “profitably grow the business together.”

The global smart connected tires market reached $18.5 billion in 2025, according to a market intelligence study by Radial Insights. The firm projects growth from $20.5 billion in 2026 to $54.2 billion by 2035. That represents a compound annual growth rate of 11.41% during the forecast period.

Tires are becoming data-producing assets as fleets and automakers integrate pressure, temperature, identification and tread information into vehicle-management systems. The market is moving beyond conventional TPMS toward predictive analytics that can estimate tire condition and reduce roadside failures. These systems also support energy efficiency and feed vehicle-control systems.
Commercial fleets provide the clearest near-term business case. Meanwhile, premium passenger vehicles and software-defined platforms create a second high-value growth channel.
Smart Connected Tires Market Study Examines Technologies

The 231-page study evaluates demand by end user, technology, application, connectivity, vehicle type and data platform. It covers embedded RFID, pressure and temperature sensors, tread-wear sensing, Bluetooth and cellular connectivity. The study also examines OEM proprietary platforms, third-party fleet analytics and predictive-maintenance applications.
Fleet Economics Make Predictive Tire Monitoring a Core Use Case

Commercial fleets are adopting connected-tire systems because tire condition directly affects roadside downtime, fuel or energy use and replacement timing. Real-time pressure and temperature data help maintenance teams identify problems before they become service events. Meanwhile, centralized analytics can reduce the need for manual inspection across large vehicle populations.
Radial Insights cites Michelin Connected Fleet pilots in which Smart Predictive Tire reduced emergency roadside events by 80%. The pilots also demonstrated a 4% reduction in fuel consumption.
The economics are strongest in long-haul, regional and last-mile fleets. High annual mileage magnifies every avoided service call and every incremental efficiency gain.

The connected model also changes the revenue relationship. Tire makers can combine products with monitoring subscriptions, analytics and service support. This creates recurring digital revenue and stronger customer retention than a standalone tire sale.
Smart Tires Move Deeper Into Vehicle Control and Safety Systems

Connected tires are beginning to provide information that can support more than maintenance. Friction, load and road-condition estimates can become inputs for braking, stability control and advanced driver-assistance systems. This becomes increasingly important as vehicles become more software-defined.

Pirelli Cyber Tyre demonstrates this direction by transmitting tire information directly into vehicle electronics. Meanwhile, Goodyear has integrated SightLine with vehicle-control software platforms.

Michelin’s universal tire digital-twin approach shows another path. It uses vehicle data and algorithms to estimate tire condition without requiring every function to depend on additional tire-mounted hardware.

This shift raises the strategic value of tire data. Suppliers can move higher in the mobility software stack by delivering accurate analytics and secure integration with vehicle systems. They can also create partnerships that are more difficult to displace than conventional product-supply contracts.

The Audi valvelift system, or AVS, is a two-stage variable-valve-lift system. Instead of changing only a camshaft’s angular position, AVS changes the lobe that operates the intake, exhaust or both valves. A small or short-duration profile reduces pumping losses at partial load; while a larger profile improves cylinder filling or exhaust flow under load. Some versions add a zero-lift profile for cylinder deactivation.

AVS first appeared globally on Audi’s 2.8-liter FSI V6 and reached North America on the 3.2-liter FSI V6 for 2008. Audi subsequently used it on some 2.0 TFSI EA888 four-cylinders; the 2.5 TFSI EA855 evo; 2.9- and turbocharged 3.0-liter EA839 V6 engines; 4.0 TFSI V8s; the second-generation 5.2 FSI V10; and the 6.3 FSI W12. European applications include the 1.4 TFSI cylinder-on-demand engine and 4.0 TDI V8. The supercharged EA837 3.0 TFSI is an important exception: Audi states that it does not use AVS.

Volkswagen-brand applications include the intake-side system on the EA888 Generation III B 2.0 TSI introduced in the 2018 Tiguan and related B-cycle applications. European 1.4- and 1.5-liter TSI engines use the sliding-cam principle for Active Cylinder Technology, or ACT. Equipment varies by output, market and engine code, so never identify AVS by displacement or badge alone.

AVS can be installed on either side. The longitudinal Audi EA888 2.0 TFSI originally used AVS on its single exhaust camshaft. Volkswagen’s EA888 Generation III B uses it on the intake camshaft. A V6 may have it on one intake camshaft per bank, or two camshafts. Cylinder-deactivation V8 and V10 versions switch both intake and exhaust valves on the affected cylinders, sealing them with all valves closed.

The basic camshaft carries external splines. Cylindrical cam pieces, sometimes called cam sleeves, fit over those splines and carry two or more adjacent lobe profiles. Electromagnetic actuators are mounted in the cam cover or camshaft frame above the sleeves.

When the ECM commands a change, it briefly energizes an actuator and extends a metal pin into a helical groove in the rotating cam piece. The groove converts rotation into axial movement, sliding the sleeve until the alternate lobe aligns with the follower. A spring-loaded detent holds the sleeve, and a return ramp pushes the actuator pin back, inducing a voltage pulse that confirms the shift. A second actuator and groove move the sleeve in the opposite direction.

AVS and variable valve timing are separate systems. AVS changes lift and duration by selecting lobes. A hydraulic camshaft adjuster rotates the entire camshaft relative to the crankshaft, changing when the valves open and close. The ECM coordinates both with throttle angle, load, speed, boost and temperature.

On an intake-side B-cycle engine, the small profile provides a shorter opening period and earlier closing point. Cam phasing positions that event. Under higher load, AVS selects the longer profile and the phaser moves toward an Otto-cycle strategy. Exhaust-side systems coordinate lift, duration and cam position to manage residual gas, turbine energy and cylinder filling.

On exhaust-side applications, it selects the valve event that preserves exhaust-pulse energy and gas velocity at lower speed, helping the turbine respond sooner. At higher airflow, the larger, longer-duration profile reduces restriction. The ECM coordinates AVS with cam phasing, ignition, throttle and wastegate control; the benefit comes from the complete charge-management strategy.

The sleeve is not shifted by engine oil. The actuator is electrical, and camshaft rotation supplies the force that moves the sleeve. However, oil is still essential for lubricating the cam pieces, splines, followers and bearings. More importantly, the conventional cam phasers paired with AVS are hydraulically operated. Incorrect viscosity, low oil pressure, sludge or aeration can therefore cause timing faults or poor operation that may be mistaken for an AVS failure.

Common complaints include a MIL or EPC lamp, rough operation, reduced power and valve-lift actuator codes. Depending on the application, technicians may encounter P11A1 through P11B8 electrical or implausible-signal faults. Likely causes include an open or shorted actuator coil, connector or harness damage, incorrect actuator-to-cam clearance, a sticking actuator pin, or a cam piece that cannot slide because of wear, damage or contamination.

Audi TSB 2031085/1 addresses implausible cam-actuator signals on 2009-2012 3.2 FSI applications. It calls for measuring actuator-pin clearance and specifies a revised actuator at 0.9 mm or greater; Audi also noted an optimized camshaft frame from July 2011.

When working on this, start diagnosis with a full scan, freeze-frame data and the appropriate output test or basic setting. Confirm power, ground and coil integrity before condemning the camshaft, and separate AVS codes from cam-phaser or oil-pressure faults.

The BMW N54 is known for its smooth power delivery, nearly nonexistent turbo lag and robust forged internals. It’s also known to suffer from a few common issues, one of which is its electric water pump. That’s right, the water pump, the component that circulates coolant throughout the engine cooling circuit, is electric.

The water pumps we’re discussing are used in a number of vehicles. This includes the 128i, 325i, 325xi, 330i, 330xi, 525i, 525xi, 528i, 528xi, 530i, 530xi, X3, X5, and Z4. Let’s take a closer look at this unique water pump, how to replace it efficiently and what other components should be replaced along with it.

Electric water pumps are becoming more and more common on modern engines. Electric auxiliary water pumps have been around for a long time. Their job is to circulate warm coolant through the heater core or to circulate coolant throughout an additional cooling circuit, such as a water-to-air charge air cooler.

Using an electric water pump instead of the more common belt- or chain-driven mechanical pump does offer a number of advantages to both automakers and customers. The speed of a mechanical pump is directly tied to engine RPM, so the pump is able to circulate coolant only at a given rate. But since there is no mechanical link between the engine and the electric water pump, it is able to circulate coolant at whatever rate is needed based on operating conditions.

The electric water pump on the N54 has a power output of 400W, and a maximum flow rate of 9,000 liters per hour. The motor power is electronically controlled by the control module inside the pump housing, and this module is connected via the communication BUS to the Digital Motor Electrics (DME), also known as the engine control unit or ECU. The DME uses the engine load, the operating mode and the data from the temperature sensors to calculate the required cooling output, then commands the electric pump according to the current operating conditions. The electric pump regulates its speed based on this command from the DME. Coolant flows through the motor inside the pump, providing cooling to both the motor and the electronic module.
The electric water pump circulates coolant even after the engine has been shut off. Doing this can cool down the turbochargers and help to prolong their service life.
Electric water pumps on the N54 have been known to fail around 60,000-80,000 miles.

When the DME detects an issue with the pump, or if it sees engine coolant temps rising, it will notify the driver through the instrument cluster. This may take the form of one of two different messages: “Engine Temp High – Drive Moderately” displayed in yellow, or “Engine Overheat – Stop” displayed in red. The vehicle may go into “limp mode” which limits the engine RPM and available gear selection in an effort to protect engine components from damage. The electric cooling fan will usually jump to its maximum speed. You may also find stored 2E81 and/or 2E82 trouble codes, which indicate a problem with the pump.
There are two other cooling system issues you should be on the lookout for whenever you’re inspecting or quoting a replacement to a customer: The coolant inlet pipe, and the “Mickey Mouse” hose.

The coolant inlet pipe is an aluminum pipe with a rubber elbow on one end and an aluminum flange on the other end. The aluminum flange bolts up to the cylinder head between the turbochargers, and the rubber elbow connects to the water pump. The aluminum portion of this component should last for a long, long time, but the rubber elbow is prone to failing. This is largely due to the fact that it is mounted so close to the front turbocharger.

The real issue for customers is that BMW offers only the entire assembly; the hose isn’t available from the dealer separately. The hose clamp on the water pump side is a standard worm-drive unit so it’s easy to remove, but the other clamp is proprietary and it’s extremely difficult to remove without cutting it off. Worst of all, the flanged end of the pipe is tucked between the turbochargers, behind a number of heat shields and the downpipes.

All in all, it’ll take 6.7+ hours to replace this pipe, which feels like a waste if the rubber elbow is the only part that really failed. Thankfully, Rein offers the hose by itself, and it should take only an hour to install.

One of the many hoses which connects to the thermostat and water pump connects to the front of the engine just under the valve cover. This hose is commonly referred to as the “Mickey Mouse hose” due to the unique shape of the flange. This flange is made of plastic, and we all know how plastic parts can become brittle and crack after years of heat-cycling.

Just like the coolant inlet pipe, this flange is available only from BMW with the hose attached. Rein came up with a solution in the form of a metal replacement connector which can be purchased with or without the hose attached.

- Broad vehicle coverage: The team highlights Autel’s usefulness on a variety of vehicles, including older Mercedes-Benz models and Porsche vehicles where access to or compatibility with OE tools can be challenging.
- Advanced diagnostic capabilities: Bidirectional controls and live data allow technicians to go beyond calibration and investigate why a system is failing.

- Real-world radar diagnosis: On a 2024 Mazda CX-5, the team used Autel data to identify an internally damaged radar sensor after calibration attempts failed, helping document the necessary repair and return the vehicle to pre-loss condition.
- Remote technical support: National Calibration can remotely access the diagnostic equipment to assist technicians with difficult vehicles and calibration problems.

- Better documentation: Capturing diagnostic data throughout the repair creates a clear record of the procedures performed, findings and final results, which can also support conversations with insurers.

- Keeping pace with vehicle technology: Ongoing software updates, technical support and technician feedback help shops maximize their equipment investment while adapting to changing ADAS and diagnostic requirements.

The Cruisin’ Morro Bay Car Show presented a $2,000 donation to the Morro Bay High School Automotive Program and ASB Auto Club Tuesday, supporting students as they compete, travel and continue their automotive education beyond high school.

Cruisin’ Morro Bay Car Show representative Ken Vesterfelt presented the donation at the MBHS automotive shop alongside Auto Club students, community supporters and leadership from Morro Bay High School and the San Luis Coastal Unified School District.

The donation will support team uniforms, student meals and travel expenses for Auto Club activities and competitions. Funds will also help provide tools for students who continue their automotive education at Cuesta College, helping bridge the transition from high school automotive education to college and the workforce.

“This support makes a direct difference for our students,” said Ritchie Wimmer, MBHS Automotive Technology Instructor. “It helps us give students experiences outside the classroom today while also helping them take the next step into college, technical training and the automotive industry.”

The timing of the presentation put that support into action immediately. Later Tuesday, members of the MBHS Auto Club Kart Racing Team were scheduled to travel to K1 Speed in Clovis to compete in Round 10 of the Teen Challenge GP.
The presentation was attended by Dr. Eric Prater, SLCUSD Superintendent; Dan Neff, SLCUSD Secondary Director; and Michael Franklin, MBHS Principal, along with students and community supporters.

The MBHS Automotive Program combines classroom instruction, hands-on shop experience, competition and career-connected learning. Through the ASB Auto Club, students also participate in kart racing, automotive events and other activities that provide opportunities to develop teamwork and professional skills beyond the classroom.
For Wimmer, the donation also demonstrates to students that Morro Bay’s automotive community is invested in their future.

“When students see organizations like the Cruisin’ Morro Bay Car Show supporting them, they see that the community values what they’re working toward,” Wimmer said. “Whether they’re representing MBHS at a competition or heading to Cuesta College to continue their automotive education, we want them to know there are people behind them.”

Morro Bay High School and the MBHS Automotive Program thank Vesterfelt and the Cruisin’ Morro Bay Car Show, including its organizers, volunteers, participants and sponsors, for their continued investment in local students.

For decades, cylinder head development has largely been discussed in terms of airflow. Bigger ports, better chambers, improved valve jobs, optimized cross-sectional area and increasingly sophisticated CNC programs have all helped engine builders move more air through an engine. But eventually, improving the cylinder head itself runs into a fundamental problem: everything surrounding the cylinder head has to cooperate.
For Scott Patton and the team at M&M Competition Engines, that realization has increasingly pushed cylinder head development into another area – valvetrain geometry.

Rather than design a port and then figure out how to package the rocker arms, pushrods, lifters and valves around it, M&M approaches cylinder head development almost from the opposite direction. Determine where the valves need to be, determine where the valvetrain needs to be and then give the port the best possible environment within those parameters.
“Everything, all the fancy terms, all the development – all you’re trying to do is make that pushrod straight,” Patton says. “When that pushrod’s straight, everything is happy.”
Getting there can require rethinking decades of conventional cylinder head and engine architecture.

Patton’s perspective on cylinder head development comes partially from M&M’s history as an engine builder. Although the company has shifted toward machining, design and manufacturing, those years assembling complete engines influence how M&M approaches new components.
“Everything we design, whether it’s a cylinder head, intake, or a block, we think about the whole package instead of just the one item,” Patton states.

That distinction becomes especially important with the valvetrain. A cylinder head can have tremendous airflow potential, but the physical location of its ports, valves and pushrods has consequences throughout the engine.
Patton says M&M starts a cylinder head project by identifying what the company calls the “non-negotiables.”

“You’ve got things such as your head-bolt pattern. You can’t change that,” Patton points out. “You’ve got your bore center. You can’t change that. In many instances, you can’t change lifter location. You’ve got, in some instances, valve cover design, you can’t change that. Some class rules require certain port heights, so you can’t change that.”
Those fixed dimensions create the box in which the cylinder head designer has to operate. The interesting part, according to Patton, is what happens next.

“We take all the non-negotiables and that’s where we start our design process,” he says. “From there, we then concentrate on your valvetrain, because in our opinion, the valvetrain is the single non-negotiable that you can actually change.”

A lifter may be locked into a particular position because of the block, for example, but rocker placement can potentially be altered. Valve locations and angles can be reconsidered. Pushrod placement can change. Once those pieces start moving, the designer suddenly has more control over the entire path between the camshaft and valve.

The ultimate target is a pushrod that operates as straight as possible both side-to-side and front-to-back. Once that position is established, M&M can develop the intake port around the available pushrod window rather than doing the reverse.
“Most people who design heads will design the port and then try to force the pushrods in the engine,” Patton says. “And that just isn’t really the right way to do it.”
Designing the valvetrain first doesn’t literally mean M&M begins by placing the rocker arms on a blank CAD model. Valve location and valvetrain geometry have to evolve together.

“You can’t necessarily get your rocker in the correct placement without locating your valve first, which we spend a lot of time on,” Patton says. “That actually goes hand-in-hand simultaneously with the valvetrain development.”

That can make valve placement one of the most time-consuming portions of a new cylinder head project. Patton says M&M may spend anywhere from two weeks to a month simply determining the proper valve locations. One of the critical dimensions is the valve’s “pierce point” – where the valve centerline intersects the deck surface.
Where that point resides relative to the bore and how the valve is rotated can influence numerous other dimensions within the cylinder head.
“That affects everything depending on how you’re rotating your valves and where that valve is in relationship to the center of the bore,” he says.

The process illustrates why valve angle should not simply be viewed as a specification on a cylinder head catalog. Moving from a 23-degree arrangement to 17 degrees or 15 degrees, for example, changes considerably more than the angle at which the valve sits in the chamber.

M&M is currently demonstrating that flexibility with its conventional-style aluminum big block Chevy cylinder head casting. The latest version was driven by a 485 cid truck pulling application. The prevailing combination in that class has been a larger-bore, shorter-stroke engine. M&M wanted to approach the combination differently, using a smaller bore and longer stroke. That decision meant its existing cylinder head designs, intended for bore sizes of roughly 4.600” or larger, were no longer ideal.

The resulting head is designed around a 4.375” bore. That smaller bore requires smaller valves, but Patton says M&M is still targeting the same airflow as the larger-bore combination. At the same time, the smaller port cross-sectional area combined with the longer-stroke engine is intended to significantly improve torque while maintaining comparable horsepower.

It’s a good example of why cylinder head geometry cannot be separated from the engine beneath it. Bore, stroke, valve location, valve diameter, port area and valvetrain geometry are all pieces of the same combination.
There is still a major limitation to this approach – the block. M&M ran into that reality years ago while developing billet cylinder heads for 400 cid Pro Stock applications.
“Cylinder heads – I don’t want to say they’ve reached their potential or their pinnacle – but they’ve gone as far as the block underneath them will allow them to go,” Patton says.

Roughly 15 years ago, M&M began experimenting with changing the block architecture to give its cylinder heads and valvetrain additional freedom. At the time, that meant taking an existing Dart block, cutting away a significant portion of it, welding in a tube and physically relocating components. Today, those concepts have found their way into M&M’s EOS cast block.

One of the most significant changes is the camshaft location. The EOS uses a 1.053” raised cam location – considerably higher than the traditional small block Chevy position. The reason was initially to provide room for a larger cam core without cutting into the cylinder walls.The block can accommodate up to a 70mm roller bearing, but M&M went considerably further.

Four additional cam bearing housing bores were incorporated into the casting, allowing as many as nine cam bearing locations. Additional material was also placed around the lifter bores, allowing substantially larger lifter bushings without breaking into water.
Those changes suddenly give a cylinder head and valvetrain designer options that previously did not exist. One SB2.2-based project demonstrates the potential.

The engine was being built using an EOS block, and the desired lifter locations interfered with the conventional small block Chevy cam bearing positions. On a traditional block, that creates a significant problem. A lifter cannot simply occupy the same physical space as a cam bearing.
With the EOS, M&M eliminated the three conventional center cam bearing locations and added four bearings in different positions. The finished combination uses six cam bearings.

Because the larger cam tunnel can be machined as a continuous cylindrical housing bore, M&M can position those bearings according to the needs of the particular engine rather than allowing traditional cam bearing locations to dictate lifter placement. This helps put that pushrod straight up and down.

For that particular engine, the changes created nearly 4” of separation between the lifters on each cylinder despite retaining a 4.400” bore center. That is an enormous amount of freedom within a small-block package. Patton believes that freedom could ultimately affect cylinder head development beyond M&M itself.
This sort of out-of-the-box thinking has also crept into M&M’s small block billet cylinder heads, where they have two different lifter patterns that the shop can make its heads on.

“We realize that a lot of people want to put our heads on existing engines that they’ve got out there, and they don’t want to go out and spend another $4,000-$10,000 on a block just to change the lifter pattern on it,” Patton says. “What we typically do is design multi-use cases on our cylinder heads to where you can put it on a normal, small block Chevrolet inline lifter pattern. Or, we do have a revised lifter location that changes some things around that makes it even that much better.”

These changes and options M&M has developed take into consideration all sorts of engine platforms and applications, which means different outside forces can handcuff your options, but nonetheless, M&M is always considering how it can make valvetrain better.
Manufacturing Makes New Geometry Possible
None of this development would be particularly useful if the designs could not be manufactured accurately and repeatedly.
M&M’s transition from traditional engine building toward component manufacturing has therefore gone hand-in-hand with its ability to manipulate cylinder head and valvetrain architecture.

Its early billet cylinder head work illustrates just how dramatically the process has changed. M&M’s first billet cylinder head, the Revolution, originated partly from frustration with traditional splayed-valve small-block designs. Looking at the relationship between the intake manifold and intake valves, Patton and his team questioned why they were working so hard to turn incoming air toward the ports. Their solution was anything but conventional.
“Why don’t we just flip these valves around, put the intake where the exhaust was and the exhaust where the intake was?” Patton recalls.
Doing so pointed the intake ports toward the center of the engine and better aligned them with the intake manifold.
“We now do 100% of the entire design in CAD,” Patton says. “That enables us to do so much testing before we even cut our first chip.”

Patton estimates CAD allows M&M to get approximately 97% to 98% of the way toward a finished design. Real-world testing still determines that final few percent, but digital development allows the team to uncover interference issues and concepts that simply will not work before committing expensive material and machining time.

Once a design reaches production, M&M relies heavily on a Haas UMC 1000P five-axis machining center. Patton says the machine is particularly well suited to cylinder head manufacturing and has helped move M&M to another level of production.

The combination of CAD development and five-axis machining becomes especially important as valve angles, rocker locations and port architecture become less conventional. Complex geometry is only valuable if it can be transferred from a computer model into a repeatable component.

Cylinder head development is unlikely to stop being about airflow. Port velocity, cross-sectional area, valve sizing and chamber design will remain critical to making power. But the next gains may increasingly come from looking beyond the port itself.

For M&M, that means considering the cylinder head as part of a larger mechanical system extending all the way from the camshaft through the lifter, pushrod and rocker to the valve – and even down into the block architecture that establishes where many of those components can physically reside.
It also means questioning dimensions that have traditionally been treated as fixed simply because they have existed for decades.

The EOS block grew from ideas M&M experimented with approximately 15 years ago because existing blocks were beginning to dictate how far its cylinder heads could evolve. The company’s billet heads have challenged conventional valve arrangements. Its current big block development is moving valve angles and valve sizes to better suit a smaller-bore, longer-stroke combination.
The common thread is not change simply for the sake of change. It is creating a better mechanical relationship between all pieces.

That philosophy may be particularly relevant as racing engines continue to demand greater rpm, airflow and output from architectures that, in some cases, trace their basic dimensions back 40 or 50 years.
Instead of asking how much more port can be squeezed around an existing pushrod, the better question may be whether the pushrod belongs there in the first place.

For Patton, that is where cylinder head development starts getting interesting. Once the fixed dimensions have been identified, everything else becomes an opportunity. Sometimes making more power begins with something as seemingly simple as making the pushrod straight.

U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler (R-District 17) has filed a bill that would require auto dealerships and other resale channels selling used vehicles to sell them with functional airbag systems, or if an airbag is missing or disabled, to clearly disclose that.

If passed, the bill would mean up to life in prison for sellers if someone dies as a result of a vehicle sold at an auction or dealership without disclosing the vehicle is missing an airbag or is equipped with a disabled one.
Lawler filed the Anthony Amoros Law Right to Know Act this week, according to a press release from his office.

Anthony Amoros died in 2013 at the age of 18 after crashing his car on a windy stretch of road, according to a New York CBS News report. Amoros’s family purchased the vehicle without knowing it lacked an airbag.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a bill titled “Anthony Amoros Law” in 2021 that prohibits used car dealers from selling vehicles without a working airbag, according to Spectrum News. The law requires sellers to provide consumers with certification that the vehicle is equipped with an airbag.

“Every driver and passenger deserves to know that the vehicle they are getting into is safe, and this bill will help protect consumers by making sure they have the information they need to make informed decisions,” Lawler said in his press release. “This legislation will ensure dealerships and third-party sellers cannot sell these vehicles without clearly informing consumers of the safety risks.”
Lawler’s bill would require sellers to disclose that vehicles don’t have a working airbag on the front of the sales contract receipt and invoice.
The proposed law would give state officials or agencies authority to regulate and enforce compliance after Federal Trade Commission (FTC) notice.
The FTC will have the right to intervene in any action or file a petition of appeal.
Penalties outlined in the bill allow for a court to award an additional $25,000 for an action that involves death or paralysis.
The bill states that those who knowingly sell a vehicle without a working airbag and disclosure could be fined and face up to 10 years in prison.
It adds that a seller could face up to 20 years in prison if someone is seriously injured, including paralysis.
The bill also defines a “deficiency” as a vehicle without a functional airbag system and/or inflatable restraint system.

Counterfeit airbags are not specifically mentioned in the bill. However, it’s likely that vehicles without an airbag or a deficient airbag system travel through the same salvage routes as vehicles with counterfeit airbags.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recently identified an 11th death caused by a counterfeit airbag part that the agency banned earlier this year.
The death happened Aug. 27 in Dallas, Texas, and is described as an otherwise survivable crash by NHTSA.

Teena Bohi, an Automotive Anti-Counterfeiting Council (A2C2) board member, said during a Collision Industry Conference (CIC) meeting in July that NHTSA’s investigation has uncovered how dangerous counterfeit parts find their way into vehicles.

“The totaling of a vehicle isn’t a cut-and-dried process,” Bohi says. “The value is driven depending on whether it is self-insured, the state the vehicle was in, the insurer’s own practices, processes, and thresholds. There is a lot that goes into just determining if the vehicle is totaled.”

Next, the vehicle often goes to an auction. If it is a public auction, an airbag deployment will possibly be reported to the National Motor Vehicle Title Information System (NMVTIS). The system is a database meant to prevent the resale of stolen vehicles and track unsafe salvage cars. If the vehicle goes to a wholesale or private auction, the previous crash information is not always captured, she said.

According to an Automotive News opinion piece, about 2.5 million vehicles were totaled by insurers last year before eventually returning to U.S. roadways. It says that a shift in insurers totaling more vehicles, along with the higher cost of new and used vehicles, has forced more dealers to repair and sell salvaged-titled vehicles.
Copart CEO Jeff Liaw discussed how salvaging a car for auction competes with collision repairs during a 2025 earnings call.

“Even an insurance carrier can sell their cars through other intermediaries; they can have more of them repaired,” Liaw said in the September call. “In many respects, we compete with the repair shops. The higher the returns we generate, the more we can win the rights to resolve that claim versus the repair industry. The lower the returns we generate, the more we lose head-to-head against the repair shops as well. There are a number of competitive threats that we face on any given day.”
He went on to describe how delivering “excellent service,” such as expediting cycle times and interacting with policyholders, can drive auction returns.
Those vehicles eventually have to be rebuilt before returning to the road — a process Bohi said can create opportunities for counterfeit safety components to enter the supply chain.
After repairs, vehicles are retitled, and the process can vary state to state, including the inspection process, Bohi says. Many don’t require airbag inspections.
“There are a lot of gaps where attention could be focused that could help address these types of issues,” Bohi said.
The Automotive News piece suggests that state processes, including inspection requirements, may need reworking as the market shifts to more dealers selling salvaged titles.

ASE Connects, formerly WrenchWay, now offers collision, automotive, and diesel students direct connections to shops and dealerships by creating free profiles.

Whether searching for internships, preparing for their first shop tour, or seeking a full-time job, ASE says students can use their profiles to highlight their interests, skills, experience, and career goals.

Earlier this year, ASE and WrenchWay launched ASE Connects to strengthen the technician pipeline by connecting schools and industry, expanding access to workforce data, and supporting automotive, diesel, and collision career pathways.

“Creating a free student profile gives students an opportunity to put themselves on the radar of shops and dealerships while taking an important step in their careers,” said Dave Johnson, president and CEO of ASE, in a press release. “It gives students a way to showcase who they are, what they are interested in, and where they want to go, while helping them make valuable connections and discover real-world opportunities.”
The profiles include school and program information, interests, skills, experience, and career goals. ASE Connects can also convert the profile into a résumé.

Students indicate the types of experiences they’re interested in, such as shop tours, job shadowing, internships, part-time jobs, or full-time employment. Shops and dealerships can then discover student profiles and reach out directly when they see a potential fit.

“A service professional career can start with one connection,” said Johnson. “A free student profile provides students with a simple way to start making those connections and explore opportunities that can help launch their careers.”
Students can create a free ASE Connects account and student profile here or by downloading the ASE Connects mobile app.

The U.S. economy is short roughly 140,000 skilled technicians a year, and the gap is widening, with 73,354 new collision repair entrant technicians needed by 2029, according to the TechForce Foundation’s latest “Technician Supply, Demand & Opportunity Report.”

Collision/autobody program completions have grown 14.2% year over year to 5,462, the strongest growth rate of any sector. Only 325 institutions offer collision programs nationally. Texas leads completions at 11.2%.

“Pipeline expansion without retention reform will not solve the shortage,” the report states. “Industry must invest in the conditions that keep technicians engaged, including comprehensive benefits, clear career pathways, modern tools, and workplace cultures that support long-term success. You cannot solve a shortage if you cannot keep the people you train.”
Hurricane Isias is expected to bring heavy rainfall to the central U.S. Gulf Coast and much of the Southeast Friday and into the weekend, according to the National Hurricane Center (NHC).
NHC told the area to prepare for considerable flash and urban flooding, along with significant river flooding, gusty winds, and areas of heavy rain in the western portion of the Yucatan Peninsula.
To get ready for Isaias, GEICO urges customers in the storm’s potential path to take these steps:
- “Follow guidance from local emergency officials, including any evacuation orders.
- “Create an evacuation plan ahead of time. Identify a safe place outside the storm’s path and designate a key contact to share evacuation plans.
- “Move vehicles out of low-lying areas. Vehicles that aren’t being used to evacuate should be moved away from areas prone to heavy flooding. If possible, use a garage or covered parking.
- “Fill the tank. Make sure all vehicles have a full tank of gas.
- “Build a disaster kit. Include three days of water, medications, toiletries, charging cables, blankets, batteries, and a radio. Add food as needed, plus supplies for pets.
- “Identify a safe place for key vehicle documents. If you need to file a claim, have your vehicle title, registration, and any lienholder information handy.”

Consumers are encouraged to download insurance company mobile apps to access policy documents and file a claim, according to a GEICO press release. Consumers may also want to add insurance company 800 numbers to their contacts.
After a storm, consumers should use extreme caution as wind and flooding damage could be severe. The insurance company notes that cars may have been submerged in floodwaters that have since receded.
“Don’t try to drive a vehicle you suspect was flooded,” the release adds.
It also warns consumers to stay away from their vehicle if downed power lines are nearby.
Consumers should leave their vehicles in place if heavy debris, such as a tree limb, falls on them, the release adds. It says the debris could pose a safety risk.

“In situations with major safety risks, GEICO’s claims team will work with customers and come directly to them to inspect a vehicle that isn’t drivable,” the release states. “Customers just need to file a claim first, and GEICO will then work with them to set up a field inspection appointment as quickly as possible.”

Resources are available to anyone who works in the industry. This includes individuals working in shops or in supporting roles outside of a shop.
The organization does not provide funds for businesses. However, a business owner can apply for funds for items, like personally owned tools.
To apply for assistance, click here. Businesses may wish to broadcast the resource to any employee or family impacted by the storm.

Together, we can build a rock-solid safety net for colleagues recovering from natural disasters and life-altering emergencies.”

When we talk about safety in the collision repair industry, the conversation often centers on obvious hazards: welding temperatures, sparks, fumes, electricity, sharp metal, and the importance of wearing the proper personal protective equipment. Those risks are critical to address, but there is another category of safety that can be easier to overlook because the damage isn’t always immediate: ergonomics.

Collision repair is physically demanding work. Technicians spend hours lifting, reaching, bending, twisting, kneeling, working overhead, and handling heavy equipment. The cumulative effect of those movements can take a serious toll over time. In fact, roughly 20%—or 1 out of every 5—of all reported non-fatal injuries in this sector are attributed to repetitive motion or cumulative trauma (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

That statistic is a reminder that technician safety isn’t just about preventing the accident that happens today. It’s also about reducing the physical strain that can contribute to injuries over weeks, months, and years. The best shops should constantly be asking: How can we make this job safer and easier for the technician?
Invest in Your Technicians with Ergonomic Equipment
A technician’s body is one of the most important tools in the shop. Just like any other piece of equipment, it needs to be taken care of.

Consider the number of times a technician may use a spot welding gun throughout a typical day. Spot welders can be heavy, and holding that weight repeatedly—especially while reaching into awkward areas of a vehicle—can put significant stress on the shoulders, arms, wrists, and back.
One individual weld may not seem like a major physical challenge. Hundreds of welds performed over the course of a day are a different story. This is where

ergonomic equipment can make a meaningful difference. Instead of asking a technician to carry and support the full weight of a welding gun throughout the repair, equipment such as Pro Spot’s Ergo Lift Assist can help support the gun and reduce the physical load on the technician.

The technician still controls the equipment and performs the repair, but the equipment helps carry some of the burden. A technician should be focused on getting the correct weld, following the OEM procedure, preparing the metal properly, and completing a quality repair—not thinking about how much their shoulders hurt from holding a welding gun all afternoon.

Ergonomics doesn’t have to mean completely redesigning a shop. Sometimes the biggest improvements come from looking at the repetitive tasks technicians perform every day and asking where unnecessary physical effort can be eliminated.
How often are technicians lifting heavy tools?
How often are they reaching across a vehicle?
Are they bending or kneeling when the job could be positioned differently?
Are tools balanced and easy to maneuver?
Could an assist device support some of the weight?
These questions can identify opportunities to make a technician’s workday safer and more comfortable.
And because these movements are repeated hundreds or thousands of times over a career, even a small reduction in physical strain can have a significant long-term impact.
PPE and Safe Work Practices Still Matter
Ergonomics is only one part of a comprehensive safety program.

Technicians still need the proper personal protective equipment for the job, including appropriate eye and face protection, gloves, hearing protection, respiratory protection, and other PPE when required.

Welding equipment should be properly maintained and operated according to manufacturer instructions. Technicians should understand the hazards associated with welding, sparks, heat, fumes, electricity, and the materials they are working with.
OEM repair procedures should also be followed carefully. The right equipment and ergonomic setup don’t replace proper training or safe work practices.
Instead, ergonomics should complement them.
A truly safe shop addresses both the immediate hazards of the job and the long-term physical demands placed on the people performing it.
Protect the Technician, Protect the Business
Keeping technicians safe isn’t just the right thing to do. It also makes good business sense.
Skilled collision repair technicians are difficult to replace. When a technician is unavailable because of an injury or chronic physical strain, the impact can extend well beyond that individual.

Production can slow down. Other technicians may have to pick up the additional workload. Repair schedules can be affected. And the shop loses the experience and expertise of someone who may have spent years developing their skills.
Investing in ergonomics is an investment in keeping those technicians healthy and productive.
It can also send an important message to employees: We value you enough to invest in making your job safer and easier.
There’s an old saying in sports: “The best ability is availability.”
The same principle applies in the body shop.

Even the best technicians can’t perform at their best if they’re constantly dealing with fatigue, soreness, or an injury. No shop benefits from equipment or processes that unnecessarily wear down the people who rely on them every day.
The objective isn’t to make technicians work harder. It’s to give them the tools and environment they need to work smarter, safer, and more efficiently.

Ergonomic equipment such as lift assists can take some of the physical burden out of repetitive tasks. Proper PPE and safety practices help protect technicians from the immediate hazards of the shop. Together, they create an environment where technicians can focus their energy on what matters most: performing high-quality repairs.
Because protecting your technicians isn’t just about keeping them safe today.
It’s about keeping them healthy, productive, and available to do their best work tomorrow.

How Paper-Based Friction Materials Power Modern Machinery

Have you ever wondered what enables everything from roaring construction machinery to agricultural machinery plowing the fields to industrial equipment shuttling through factories—the precise starting, smooth operation, and reliable braking they achieve?

The answer lies in a seemingly insignificant yet crucial core component: friction material. It acts as the "safety guard" and "power link" of machinery, ensuring every brake is safe and effective, and every power transmission is smooth and flawless.

Among the vast family of friction materials, wet friction materials are becoming the new favorite in modern machinery due to their exceptional reliability, safety, and exceptionally long lifespan. Among wet materials, paper-based friction materials stand out as a leading force thanks to their excellent overall performance, cost-effectiveness, and broad application prospects.
Today, let's delve deeper into the fascinating world of this "unsung hero"—paper-based friction materials.
What is Paper-Based Friction Material? — A Sponge-Like Power Core
Imagine a "sponge" with countless tiny pores—that's the most intuitive image of paper-based friction material.

It is a material with a reticular porous structure composed of three core components: reinforcing fibers, functional fillers, and a binder resin. This unique structure gives it extraordinary capabilities:
- Oil Storage Capacity: The porous structure acts like a miniature "oil depot," capable of storing large quantities of lubricant.

- Dynamic Lubrication: When the friction plate and mating plate engage and are subjected to pressure, the lubricant within the material is instantly squeezed onto the friction surface, forming a tough lubricant film, enabling smooth, gentle "wet" friction.
- Self-Recovery: When the friction plates separate, the material rebounds like memory foam, "absorbing" the lubricant back into the pores, ready for the next operation.

It is this dynamic cycle of "oil storage-oil squeezing-oil return" that allows paper-based friction materials to perform well in an oil bath environment, achieving a perfect combination of high durability and stable friction performance.
Exploring Core Performance: How Do Three Key Factors Affect It?

The performance of paper-based friction materials is not static. Like a top athlete, its performance is influenced by the "field," "equipment," and "condition." Let's examine how these three key factors shape its performance.
Factor 1: The "Stage Effect" of Lubricants

Paper-based friction materials are highly sensitive to lubricants, and different lubricants create distinct "stages" for their performance. Even the same friction material can exhibit significantly different friction characteristics (especially the kinetic friction coefficient) when exposed to different lubricants.
Figure 1: Kinetic friction coefficient curve for a paper-based friction material in gear oil
Figure 2: Dynamic friction coefficient curve of the same material in hydraulic oil

Interpretation: The above chart clearly shows that the same material behaves very differently in gear oil and hydraulic fluid. Furthermore, various additives added to lubricating oils (such as dispersants and anti-wear agents) can interact complexly with the material surface, further affecting its friction properties. Therefore, choosing the right oil for paper-based friction materials is the first step in achieving optimal performance.
Density is a trump card for paper-based friction materials. It is directly related to the material's porosity, leading to a delicate balancing act in terms of performance.

High density (low porosity) means a denser material, resulting in better strength and thermal conductivity, lower wear rate, and longer life. However, the downside is reduced oil storage capacity, which can lead to a lower coefficient of friction and compromise power transmission.

Low density (high porosity) means the material is more porous, resulting in greater oil storage capacity and a higher coefficient of friction, which can provide greater braking force or transmit torque. However, the downside is reduced mechanical strength and wear resistance, shortening service life.
Figure 3: Comparison of the dynamic coefficient of friction for materials of varying densities (Type 2 to Type 6, increasing density)
Figure 4: Comparison of wear rates of materials with different densities

Interpretation: Figures 3 and 4 vividly illustrate this balancing act. There's no such thing as absolute good or bad, only suitability. When selecting a paper-based friction material, the optimal trade-off between friction coefficient and durability must be determined based on specific application requirements (e.g., high torque versus long life).
Factor 3: Extreme Challenges of Operating Conditions

In addition to oil type and density, actual operating conditions, such as surface pressure, sliding speed, and oil temperature, pose extreme challenges to paper-based friction materials. These factors directly affect the temperature of the friction interface, the thickness and stability of the oil film, and thus dynamically alter the coefficient of friction.

Therefore, please remember: the coefficient of friction of a particular paper-based friction material is not a fixed value, but rather a performance range determined through extensive and repeated testing under specific operating conditions.
Broad Applications: Injecting a Powerful "Heart" into Machinery

Thanks to its excellent overall performance and customizability, Carlisle Brake & Friction's paper-based friction materials have been successfully applied to the core components of various heavy-duty machinery, becoming their powerful and reliable "heart."
We understand that different machines and applications require significantly different friction materials. For example:
- Service brakes for construction machinery (such as excavators and loaders) require materials that provide a stable, powerful braking force under high loads to ensure safety.
- Powershift transmissions for agricultural machinery (such as tractors) require materials that provide smooth engagement and excellent heat resistance to handle frequent shifting.
- Clutches for industrial machinery require materials that respond quickly and have a long lifespan to ensure continuous and efficient operation of production lines.

To this end, Carlisle Brake & Friction has developed a series of special paper-based friction materials for different application scenarios, providing each customer with the most suitable and reliable solution.
Continuous Innovation, Driving the Future
Technological advancement is endless. To meet increasingly demanding application requirements and broaden market prospects, Carlisle Brake & Friction remains at the forefront of innovation.

We are not only continuously optimizing the formulation and processing of paper-based friction materials to push their performance limits, but are also actively exploring next-generation wet friction materials with even higher performance. These R&D efforts have made significant progress, aiming to provide global customers with more diverse and advanced options, driving the infinite possibilities of future machinery.
General Assembly adopts pandemic declaration, but not by consensus

The General Assembly on Monday adopted a political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, by 153 in favour to three against (Argentina, Israel and United States) with two abstentions (New Zealand and Paraguay).
The text was due to be approved by consensus at a high-level meeting on 25 September.
Objections from the United States and a few other States blocked that, pushing the issue back to the assembly.
Read the full political declaration here.
Chile’s representative summed up one prevailing view, saying that “no country, no matter how big it might be or how prepared it might be, can alone address a threat that knows no borders.”

The declaration is political and non-binding. It calls for stronger national, regional and international cooperation, guided by science, equity and respect for human rights, and it welcomes last year’s landmark adoption of the World Health Organization (WHO) Pandemic Agreement.

“WHO welcomes this strong commitment by UN Member States to continue working together on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response,” said World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.

“The world has come a long way since COVID-19. We urge countries to now fulfil the commitments they have made – especially to finalize negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing system (PABS) annex, so the WHO Pandemic Agreement can be opened for signature, begin the process of ratification and enter into force as international law.”
The agreement cannot be opened for signature until Member States complete the annex on pathogen access and benefit-sharing – the system by which countries would share samples and genetic data.
Those that do so would receive a share of any resulting vaccines, treatments and diagnostics.
Talks have stalled amid a standoff between developing countries and some high-income European nations together with the US.
The World Health Assembly – comprising the WHO’s 194 members – is due to return to the annex next May.
The US representative had previously cited “divisive ideologies that lack definitional consensus” as well as the declaration’s references to the continuing annex negotiations.

In addition to adopting the pandemic declaration, the 193-member world body had a number of items on its agenda on Monday, including the consideration of draft resolutions on the UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise and a political declaration of the high-level meeting to mark the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the anti-racism Durban Declaration and Programme of Action.
WHO aims to spot new outbreaks within 24 hours
The World Health Organization (WHO) on Monday launched a five-year strategy for its Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, with the goal of detecting emerging health threats within 24 hours.

Set up in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, the hub wants every country to be able to identify and understand new threats quickly, so outbreaks can be contained before they become epidemics or spread internationally.
Colombia peace deal must endure as insecurity grows, Security Council hears

Nearly 10 years after Colombia signed a historic peace agreement to end a decades-long insurgency, the deal is under strain from growing insecurity – and the UN’s top official in the country says it cannot be allowed to falter.

Miroslav Jenča told the Security Council on Monday that the 2016 accord must be implemented in full, with proper funding, better coordination between institutions and protection for former combatants.

He pointed to real gains: rural development, and mechanisms for transitional justice and reparation for victims. But he admitted that implementation has had “many shortcomings” and that much remains to be done.
Security policy and the peace agreement should reinforce each other, Mr. Jenča said, and the accord should be carried out comprehensively.

“We look forward to the further definition of its policies, and we stand ready to support the Government in this regard,” he said, offering the experience gained by the UN Verification Mission over almost a decade of supporting implementation.

Communities in conflict-affected regions remain exposed to armed groups, geographical isolation and limited access to public services. Child recruitment, particularly among ethnic communities, and threats and attacks against women remain major concerns, ambassadors heard.
Government data presented to legislators show that illegal armed groups grew from around 15,000 members in 2022 to approximately 28,000 today.
Mr. Jenča also condemned the killings of civil society leaders María Ovidia Palechor and James Flor in Cauca on 1 September, highlighting the risks faced by rights defenders.
He said expanding economic opportunities, improving public services and strengthening local institutions were essential to reducing violence.
Despite these challenges, more than 11,000 former members of the FARC-EP rebel group remain committed to reintegration.
With State and international support, they have developed around 6,000 productive projects and 300 cooperatives in sectors including agriculture, tourism, trade and textiles.
Mr. Jenča highlighted tourism initiatives involving former combatants and victims, aimed at stimulating local economies and job markets.
However, economic sustainability and security remain significant challenges. Since the agreement was signed in 2016, 501 former combatants have been killed, most recently on 22 September in Cesar.

The Special Representative reaffirmed the UN mission's readiness to continue supporting implementation and highlighted its value on the ground, noting that over almost a decade it had built relationships of trust in some of regions most impacted by continuing violence.
Colombia had entered “a new political chapter, with wide ranging challenges ahead,” Mr. Jenča said, calling for “sustained international engagement in order to overcome remaining obstacles.”
